source: Han, Ransom, Perfors, Kemp (2023) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models
finding: Tested GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on 11 Osherson property-induction phenomena (similarity, typicality, diversity, monotonicity, non-monotonicity and more). GPT-4 matched the human direction on all but one phenomenon: specific non-monotonicity.
numbers: Exp 1: 792 argument pairs (11 phenomena x 3 domains x 24 pairs; mammals, birds, vehicles). 120 MTurk people recruited, 10 excluded, N=110; about 9.2 human ratings per cell. Sign tests per 33 phenomenon-domain cells.
limits: One lab. GPT-4 snapshot 0314, forced choice on a 6-point scale. Non-monotonicity is the one failure. Humans are only mildly reliable on some phenomena (asymmetry, inclusion fallacy).
agent_relevance: Plain GPT-4 already follows similarity, typicality and diversity cues. We do not need to hand-code the similarity-coverage model for easy cases. We do need a check for cases where the premise set was chosen by someone with a goal.

source: Han, Ransom, Perfors, Kemp (2023) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models
finding: Non-monotonicity fails because the model ignores why the premises were picked. A helpful teacher would not add 'rabbit' to {crow, peacock} when the target is birds, so adding it signals a wider claim. GPT-4 treats more premises as stronger anyway.
numbers: Example: {crow, peacock, rabbit} -> bird is judged weaker than {crow, peacock} -> bird by people. GPT-4 went the other way for the Specific type.
limits: The sampling-assumption explanation (Ransom et al. 2016) is the authors' reading. It was not tested by manipulating the model's assumptions in this paper.
agent_relevance: Add a slot: 'who chose these examples and why' before treating examples as a random sample. Links to strong versus weak sampling (see c17).

source: Han, Ransom, Perfors, Kemp (2023) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models
finding: Prompt design mattered. They built a space of 288 prompt combinations (system message, context, answer format, question) and tested a hand-picked subset: a baseline matching the human task, a more specific system message, a chain-of-thought direction, and a domain-reasoning direction. The best Exp 1 prompt was the one with the chain-of-thought direction.
numbers: Best Exp 1 prompt label S3-C1-A1-Q3-O1. For Exp 2 the best prompt gave the model practice trials including its own earlier answers. Chosen by sign test across 33 splits.
limits: Best prompt chosen on the same data it was reported on (selection effect). Only GPT-4 got prompt tuning. The prompt tuned for chat models failed on models without instruction tuning (Appendix D). No single percentage gain is given in the text I read.
agent_relevance: A short reasoning direction plus worked practice trials was the best scaffold here.

source: Han, Ransom, Perfors, Kemp (2023) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models
finding: GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003) was driven by surface features such as which argument came first. The authors' own earlier study that balanced argument order had found it capturing similarity, typicality and specificity.
numbers: Earlier study (Han et al. 2022) balanced order and reported success; this study did not balance order and found poor, bimodal performance.
limits: Footnote result, no counts. This is a prompt-order artefact, not a change in model capability.
agent_relevance: Randomise and balance option order, then average. Position sensitivity can reverse conclusions about what a model can do.

source: Han, Ransom, Perfors, Kemp (2023) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models
finding: Exp 2 (rate one argument's strength): GPT-4 nearly matched the human similarity-coverage model on specific arguments but not on general ones. For single-premise general mammal arguments GPT-4 was uncorrelated with people. GPT-3.5 beat GPT-4 on general arguments. Running the similarity-coverage model on GPT-4's own similarity ratings improved the general arguments.
numbers: Spearman correlations with human ratings, five models compared with 1000 bootstrap samples. GPT-4 similarity ratings correlated above 0.6 with human similarity in all three domains. Replication of Osherson's 36 original arguments with 40 people: Spearman 0.65, p<0.001 against the 1990 rankings.
limits: Mixed picture. Exact per-cell correlations were in figures I did not read value by value. Small human replication sample.
agent_relevance: A hybrid works: ask the model for pairwise similarity numbers, then compute coverage and argument strength in code. It beat raw GPT-4 judgments on general arguments.

source: Qiu, Jiang, Lu, et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: testing inductive reasoning capabilities of language models with hypothesis refinement (ICLR)
finding: A propose, select, refine loop with a symbolic interpreter that runs each rule on the examples. LMs are strong hypothesis proposers. The loop beat plain input-output prompting on 3 of 4 datasets.
numbers: Task accuracy (%), plain prompt vs refinement: ACRE 28.0 vs 45.0 (T=1,N=1) and 48.0 (T=1,N=5); MiniSCAN 0.0 vs 46.0 (T=3,N=1); List Functions 39.6 vs 52.0 (T=1,N=1); MiniARC 13.8 vs 3.8 to 9.2 (worse). Self-consistency (N=5) on ACRE: 29.0. Self-refine with the LM as its own interpreter: ACRE 32.0.
limits: The gain depends on a task-specific symbolic interpreter that filters rules. Self-refine without that check gave small gains. MiniARC got worse (pattern matching, text-only grids).
agent_relevance: Supports G2 and G3: the filter must be code that runs the rule. For visual pattern-matching tasks, direct prediction may beat rule induction.

source: Qiu, Jiang, Lu, et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: testing inductive reasoning capabilities of language models with hypothesis refinement (ICLR)
finding: Models cannot reliably apply the rules they wrote themselves. Rule induction accuracy was far higher than rule application by the same LM.
numbers: MiniSCAN task accuracy drops from above 80% (symbolic interpreter applies the rule) to almost zero when the LM applies its own rule.
limits: Gap is strongest on recursive tasks (MiniSCAN). Self-consistency and zero-shot chain of thought did not close it (Appendix B.3).
agent_relevance: Never let the model apply its own induced rule to new items when code can. Execute the rule.

source: Qiu, Jiang, Lu, et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: testing inductive reasoning capabilities of language models with hypothesis refinement (ICLR)
finding: Noise breaks induction. Corrupting some of 8 exemplars on List Functions lowers accuracy substantially, even one bad example. A prompt line saying some examples may be wrong helps but does not remove the loss.
numbers: Noise levels 12.5%, 25%, 50% of 8 exemplars (1, 2 or 4 examples). A small human control found both fall, with a larger relative drop for the LM (appendix C, not read in detail).
limits: Human comparison used a different setup and was not run on every condition (footnote 10).
agent_relevance: Add an explicit outlier step. Allow a rule to fit all-but-k examples rather than demanding an exact fit.

source: Qiu, Jiang, Lu, et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: testing inductive reasoning capabilities of language models with hypothesis refinement (ICLR)
finding: Refinement edits are shallow. Over iterations the model mostly adds exceptions (if-else patches) for the failing example rather than starting a new hypothesis. Human rules use commonsense verbs and real-world concepts; LM rules on MiniARC are long lists.
numbers: Qualitative. 50 tasks per dataset sampled; crowdworkers wrote human rules. Using pseudo-words as outputs on MiniSCAN also hurt performance.
limits: Qualitative only.
agent_relevance: Force a fresh-hypothesis restart when patches pile up. Otherwise refinement overfits the visible examples (G3).

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber, Goodman (2024) Hypothesis Search: inductive reasoning with language models (ICLR)
finding: GPT-4 writes natural-language hypotheses, then a program per hypothesis, then code checks each program on the training examples, with up to 3 rounds of execution feedback. This beats direct prompting and program-only prompting. The design copies Bayesian human induction (a posterior over hypotheses).
numbers: ARC (100 tasks, GPT-4): direct 17%, program only 23%, LLM-summarised hypotheses 30%, human-selected hypotheses 33%, human-written hypotheses 45%. 1D-ARC (108 tasks): direct 39.6, program only 61.1, full 73.1. List Functions (100 tasks): direct 31, program only 59, full 69. SyGuS (89 tasks): 94.3% with 8 programs.
limits: These are the figures in the PDF text I read. A search snippet of another version quoted different ARC numbers (27.5% vs 12.5% on 40 tasks), so versions differ.
agent_relevance: Template for S2 candidate rules: many hypotheses in words, one program each, tested in code. The training-set pass is only a filter, so the G3 held-out check is still needed.

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber, Goodman (2024) Hypothesis Search: inductive reasoning with language models (ICLR)
finding: Where the pipeline loses: of 64 sampled hypotheses per task, GPT-4 had a correct one for only 49 of 100 ARC tasks (human-judged). Summarising 64 into 8 sometimes dropped the correct one (28 of the 30 solved tasks had a correct pre-summary hypothesis). Of the 49 tasks, 67% (33) led to a correct program.
numbers: Execution feedback rounds 0 to 3 on ARC: summarised 24, 28, 28, 30; human-selected 26, 31, 33, 33; human-written 38, 44, 45, 45. Chain of thought without programs: 19%. GPT-3.5 mostly produced meaningless hypotheses.
limits: Human selection is not automatable as is. Gains plateau after about two feedback rounds.
agent_relevance: Do not compress the hypothesis pool with the model. Rank it by code. About two feedback rounds is a reasonable cap.

source: Greenblatt (2024) Getting 50% (SoTA) on ARC-AGI with GPT-4o
finding: Brute-force hypothesis search in code: about 8,000 Python programs per problem sampled from GPT-4o, keep those correct on all training examples, revise some using the diff between output and truth, then majority vote over survivors, top 3 submissions.
numbers: 50% on the ARC public test set; 72% on a held-out train subset where humans get 85%. With 2 submissions: 48% (test) and 70% (train). About +3 points per doubling of samples (linear in log2 of sample count). Revision fixes about 20% of the remaining incorrect.
limits: Blog post, not peer reviewed. Public test set, not the private one. Train set is easier than test. The log-linear trend cannot continue forever.
agent_relevance: Accuracy buys with log-samples. Selecting by code (pass all examples) plus vote is our G5. The ceiling is set by how well the examples filter.

source: Li, Hu, Larsen, et al. (2024) Combining induction and transduction for abstract reasoning
finding: On ARC, models trained to induce a program and models trained to predict the output directly solve largely different problems. Induction is better at precise computation and composing concepts; transduction at fuzzy perceptual concepts. Ensemble: induction first, transduction as fallback.
numbers: One test set: induction 2048 samples 18.78%, transduction beam 20 15.25%, ensemble 26.50%. Another: 11.07, 13.50, 19.50. ARC-Heavy: induction (10k samples, majority vote) 19.25%, transduction 37.50%, transduction with test-time training 43.25%. Best system 56.75% vs average human 60.2%, best humans 98%. About 9% of tasks have programs that fit train but fail test.
limits: Fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B on synthetic data, not prompt-only. Pure induction can lose to transduction.
agent_relevance: Keep a fallback route: if no hypothesis passes the check, use the direct answer but mark it unchecked (hint, not proof). The 9% fits-but-wrong figure supports G3.

source: Ellis (2023) Human-like few-shot learning via Bayesian reasoning over natural language
finding: A language model proposes natural-language concept hypotheses; a learned prior and a likelihood re-weigh them. About 50 to 100 proposals match human number-game judgments, versus over 5000 hypotheses in the original Tenenbaum model. English hypotheses fit better than Python ones. Plain GPT-4 judgments differ from humans.
numbers: Number game: human data from 8 participants (ratings 1-7). Fit is R2 on held-out test numbers. Out-of-the-box prior gives a decent fit at 50-100 proposals; tuned prior a very close fit. Run-to-run variance falls as samples rise.
limits: Fits the average of 8 people; the prior is tuned on human data. The GPT-4 comparison is one curve, no exact R2 read.
agent_relevance: A working design for S2: the LLM proposes hypotheses, code does the Bayesian weighing (size principle, hypothesis averaging). Tens of proposals are enough.

source: Bazigaran and Sohn (2025) Concept generalization in humans and large language models: insights from the number game
finding: GPT-o1-mini does not generalise from a single example in the number game. It stays anchored to the shown number. Humans and the Bayesian model do generalise. The model leans on rules and little on similarity intervals.
numbers: 255 example sets, all 100 targets, 10 trials. Best-fit rule bias 0.9 in humans, 1.0 in GPT. Mean GPT-human divergence 0.87. At 4 examples the GPT-Bayes divergence is comparable to human-Bayes; at 1 example it is far worse. GPT is best fit by maximum-likelihood inference without a prior.
limits: One reasoning model carries the main analysis. GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3 and Llama-3-8B were weaker and less structured. Workshop paper. Human data from an older dataset.
agent_relevance: With only 1 or 2 examples, do not trust the model's generalisation. Compute the generalisation set in code with a hypothesis space and size principle (G5).

source: Xiong (2026) Hypothesis generation and updating in large language models
finding: Number game with three probes: posterior prediction, hypothesis evaluation, hypothesis generation. LLM predictions are near a two-parameter Bayesian fit with a built-in strong-sampling assumption (favours narrow hypotheses). Thinking mode shifts toward the prior and weakens the size principle. The three probes disagree: evaluation picks more correct hypotheses, generation proposes simpler, narrower ones.
numbers: Eight LLMs in non-thinking mode in the main comparison, with thinking pairs. Prompt conditions: Default, Strong sampling, Weak sampling, Explicit candidate list. Strong prompt had the lowest KL from the Bayesian posterior, then Default, then Weak. Showing the candidate list did not recover the Bayesian posterior.
limits: Small abstract domain. Exact KL values were in figures I did not read numerically. The Bayesian-with-bias pattern does not extrapolate beyond the example region.
agent_relevance: Generating and judging are different skills. Use generation for breadth and a separate evaluation (ideally code) for ranking. Thinking mode is not simply more Bayesian.

source: Qiu, Sha, Allen, Kim, Linzen, van Steenkiste (2026) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in large language models
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs update beliefs poorly over repeated interaction in a preference-learning task (flight recommendations). They plateau after round 1. Chain of thought, numeric formats and 30 rounds did not fix it. Fine-tuning on the Bayesian assistant's guesses beat fine-tuning on correct answers and transferred to new tasks.
numbers: 624 simulated users, 5 rounds. Bayesian-tuned models agree with the Bayesian assistant about 80% of the time, more than original or oracle-tuned models. 48 users also served humans: humans improved more than most LLMs but stayed below the Bayesian assistant.
limits: Fine-tuning, so not a scaffold-only result. Task is preference inference, not category induction.
agent_relevance: Prompting alone does not give belief updating over rounds. Keep the posterior in code and update it there; let the model only read evidence into features.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 on classic judgment vignettes (Linda, cab base-rate problem and others). It did not show base-rate neglect on the cab problem. Small rewrites of vignettes pushed it into non-human errors.
numbers: 12 standard vignettes: 6 answered correctly and all 12 either correct or human-like errors. On adversarial rewrites, errors were not human-like. Example: 15% blue, 85% green cabs and a question about black cabs, it answered 20%. Changing the order of options changed answers.
limits: Likely training exposure to the classic vignettes (the authors say so). Old model.
agent_relevance: Test with fresh variants of every judgment item. Success on famous items shows recall, not method.

source: Yax, Anllo, Palminteri (2023) Studying and improving reasoning in humans and machines
finding: Humans vs many LLMs on new variants of Linda/Bill conjunction items and CRT. The fallacy appeared and grew in the more refined davinci models; ChatGPT and GPT-4 mostly avoided it. A step-by-step style prompt raised accuracy in davinci-003 but did not change human accuracy.
numbers: GPT-4 correct on Linda 0.98, Bill 0.99 (n=2048 questions). ChatGPT Linda correct 0.70. Reasoning prompt on davinci-003: Linda +0.39, Bill +0.32 accuracy. Example prompt gave smaller gains (Linda +0.14). Humans: Reasoning prompt no effect, example prompt helped Linda (+0.14). Joint-probability arithmetic: davinci-002/003 about 90% accurate, base davinci about 50%.
limits: Different prompt formats across model families. Humans were probably less compliant with the Reasoning instruction (their answers stayed short). No log-probs for ChatGPT and GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Probability arithmetic is solved; the fallacy is in how language is read. Put the check P(A and B) <= P(A) in code.

source: Macmillan-Scott and Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in large language models
finding: Seven LLMs on 12 cognitive tasks (including Linda, an AIDS base-rate task, Monty Hall, Wason). Most wrong answers were not the human bias error. They were illogical reasoning, or correct reasoning followed by a wrong final answer. Answers were also inconsistent across 10 repeats.
numbers: GPT-4: 69.2% correct with correct reasoning. Claude 2: 55.0%. Llama 2 7B incorrect in 77.5% of cases. GPT-3.5 human-like bias errors in 21.7% of runs (50.8% counting human-like correct ones). GPT-4 human-like (correct or incorrect) 73.3%; Llama 2 13B only 8.3%. Llama 2 70B refused in 41.7%. Each task asked 10 times at default temperature.
limits: Default parameters, no system prompt, chatbot UIs for some models. Facilitated task versions were not easier for models. Only Monty Hall and one Linda case were recognised as known problems. CogBias (c28) cites this paper as showing human-like base-rate neglect and conjunction fallacy in GPT-4; that reading does not match the text I read.
agent_relevance: Run each probability question several times and compare in code. Separate final-answer extraction from the reasoning text.

source: Alsagheer, Karanjai, Shi (2024) Comparing rationality between large language models and humans: insights and open questions
finding: Short comparison of LLMs and humans on Wason, conjunction and stereotype base-rate tasks. LLM scores are near human scores. Low evidential value.
numbers: Conjunction fallacy task: LLMs 28%, humans 33.7%. Base-rate task: humans 56%, online humans 60%, ChatGPT 50%.
limits: Scoring definition and model versions are unclear. I read the method and results lines only. Treat as weak.
agent_relevance: Do not use for design choices. Listed so later reviewers see it was checked.

source: Araya (2025) Do chains-of-thought of large language models suffer from hallucinations, cognitive biases, or phobias in Bayesian reasoning?
finding: Case study of one base-rate problem (a children's card-hiding puzzle with 90% / 20% / 10% clues) given to three reasoning models. They did not pick natural frequencies on their own. When told to use Gigerenzer's natural frequencies they used them only partly, mixed with percentages and Bayes formula, and one run reached a wrong 50% answer.
numbers: Models, Feb 2025: Gemini Flash 2.0 (run twice: one correct, one wrong on prompt 1), ChatGPT o3-mini (wrong on prompt 1, 2039 words), DeepSeek R1. Four prompts: plain; plus natural frequencies; plus whole objects (blocks); plus embodied heuristics. DeepSeek on prompt 2 reached the wrong 50% in book 3.
limits: One problem, three models, one or two runs each. Qualitative reading of chains of thought.
agent_relevance: Naming the method in the prompt is weak. Better: code builds the 1000-case count table and the model only copies given rates into it.

source: Chadimova, Jursek, Kliegr (2025) Meaningless is better: hashing bias-inducing words in LLM prompts improves performance in logical reasoning and statistical learning
finding: Replacing bias-triggering words (woman, artist, reading, cafe) in a novel Linda-style item with meaningless hash tokens cut the conjunction fallacy. Reasoning models also did well without hashing. Hashing did not reliably reduce hallucination in a frequent-itemset task.
numbers: Linda-like item, no chain of thought: ChatGPT-4 and Gemini got 0 of 20 right without hashing; ChatGPT-4 with hashing and neutral descriptions got 10 of 10. Chain-of-thought models on the original text: Gemini 2 Flash Thinking 10/10, o3-mini 6/10 (p<0.001, Cramer V 0.619 GPT, 0.925 Gemini). Frequent itemsets: chain of thought did not help GPT models; hashing did better. 680 prompts, 5 model families.
limits: 10 to 20 trials per cell; one modified item. Hashed words were chosen by looking at which words drove errors on the original prompt (fitted to the test item). Temperature 0.2.
agent_relevance: Strip representativeness cues: restate with abstract labels and ask which set contains which. Test on fresh items.

source: Peruchini and Teixeira (2024) Analyzing large language models chatbots: an experimental approach using a probability test
finding: ChatGPT and Gemini handle the famous Linda problem but do worse on a new problem of the same form (the Mary problem) that needs the same probability rule.
numbers: Qualitative exploratory tests with two chatbots; no counts read in the abstract and introduction.
limits: Small exploratory study. Abstract and introduction only.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as Binz and Schulz: classic-item success may be recall. Build fresh items to check probability reasoning.

source: Wong, Grand, Lew, Goodman, Mansinghka, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2023) From word models to world models: translating natural language to the probabilistic language of thought
finding: Rational meaning construction: the LLM only translates the problem statement into code in a probabilistic programming language; exact Bayesian inference by the program does the reasoning. Cases include the Bayesian tug-of-war, relational reasoning and social reasoning.
numbers: Mostly qualitative demonstrations with Codex-style translation. I read the abstract, introduction and framework sections only, not the experiment tables.
limits: Demonstration paper. No benchmark-scale accuracy seen. Needs a generative model for each domain.
agent_relevance: Strongest template for: model translates, code computes the probability. Matches G5 for any probability question: build a small generative program, run inference, read off the number.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan, et al. (2024) Language models, like humans, show content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: On natural language inference, syllogism validity and Wason, LMs show human-like content effects. Already covered in this series (documents 03 and 04). Only noted here for completeness.
numbers: Syllogism background cited in the paper: people said an invalid syllogism was valid about 90% of the time when the conclusion was believable. Other figures were in graphs I did not read numerically.
limits: Overlaps earlier documents. Not new for this subfield.
agent_relevance: Not new. See documents 03 and 04.

source: Huang, Zhang, Kwak, An (2026) CogBias: measuring and mitigating cognitive bias in large language models
finding: Benchmark of four bias families on three LLMs. Prompt-level debiasing helped response biases but backfired for judgment biases (which include base-rate neglect). Activation steering cut the bias score 26 to 32%.
numbers: Steering reduces bias score by 26 to 32%. Qwen lost up to 19.0 points on judgment benchmarks; Llama lost negligibly. Three LLMs, 25 downstream benchmarks.
limits: Needs open weights, so unusable on a closed-model scaffold. I read the abstract, method outline and related-work text, not every table.
agent_relevance: Warning: be-careful style prompts can backfire on judgment tasks. Use code checks, not exhortations (G1, G5).

source: Frontier LLMs still struggle with simple reasoning tasks (2025)
finding: Search snippet and a keyword grep only: an appendix shows o1 answering the original Linda puzzle with the fallacy, then answering a rewritten version with the conjunction stated plainly.
numbers: No results table read.
limits: Not read for numbers. Pointer only.
agent_relevance: Another hint of recall versus reasoning on classic items.

source: Hagendorff (2023) Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in language models, and disappeared in GPT-4
finding: Only the abstract page was read: GPT-3 shows human-like intuitive errors on CRT and semantic illusions; ChatGPT and GPT-4 avoid them. The page says version 2 was withdrawn by the author (18 Aug 2023).
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Abstract only; withdrawn version. Do not cite for numbers.
agent_relevance: Pointer only.
